body.objective: Students will be able to compare realism and non-realism.
body.iCan: I can compare realism and non-realism.
successCriteria: I can describe the features of realism and non-realism
I can compare Stanislavski and Brecht's goals
I can perform a short text in two contrasting styles
body.hook: Picture two plays. In one, a family argues around a real kitchen table and you feel like you're spying on them. In the other, an actor turns to you and says, "Don't get comfortable, this is a play, and you should be asking why this is happening." Both are powerful. They just want different things from you.

vocabulary.definition: A style that shows life as it is, aiming for the audience to believe in the characters.
Any style that breaks from showing everyday life, using symbols, exaggeration or direct address.
The imaginary wall between the stage and audience.
Epic theatre developed by Bertolt Brecht to make audiences think critically, not just feel.
Brecht's techniques that remind the audience they are watching a play.
A style showing life as meaningless or illogical, as in Beckett's "Waiting for Godot."

study.title: One Text, Two Worlds
study.question: How do realistic and non-realistic styles change how an audience experiences a story?
study.passage:
Realism (late 1800s on): Henrik Ibsen ("A Doll's House"), Anton Chekhov. Real-looking sets, everyday speech, psychological truth, a closed fourth wall. Stanislavski's system was built for this style.
Brechtian (epic) theatre (1920s on): Bertolt Brecht wanted audiences to think about social problems, not get lost in emotion. Techniques: breaking the fourth wall, placards and projected titles, narration, actors playing several roles, showing the stage machinery, songs that interrupt the action.
Absurdism (1950s on): Samuel Beckett, Eugène Ionesco. Repetitive dialogue, circular plots, strange situations, dark humour.
Activity (40 minutes): In pairs, take this short original text about a worker being laid off:
BOSS: We're making some changes.
WORKER: How many changes?
BOSS: One. You.
WORKER: Twelve years.
BOSS: And we're grateful for every one.
Version 1, Realism: Play it truthfully with objectives and subtext. Version 2, Brechtian: Add a placard ("Scene 4: Efficiency"), narrate a stage direction aloud, step out to ask the audience a question. Perform both and discuss the difference.
study.source: Original scene and activity written for this lesson; styles summarized from standard theatre history sources.
steps: Perform one text in two styles
discussion: Which version made you feel more? Which made you think more?
Why did Brecht want to interrupt emotion?
When might a director choose non-realism?
Can a production mix both styles?
study.product: Perform the same short scene in realistic and Brechtian styles and write a 300-word comparison of the techniques and their effects.

examples.answer: Stanislavski wanted belief and empathy; Brecht wanted critical thinking about society

practice.a: A style showing life as it really is.
The imaginary wall between stage and audience.
Techniques reminding the audience they are watching a play.
Placards, direct address, narration, multiple roles, visible stage machinery, songs.

practice.q: Why did Brecht want audiences to think instead of feel?
practice.a: So they would question social problems and want change.

practice.q: What are features of absurdist theatre?
practice.a: Repetition, circular plots, illogical situations, dark humour.

practice.q: What does breaking the fourth wall mean?
practice.a: Speaking directly to or acknowledging the audience.

practice.q: When might a director choose non-realism?
practice.a: To highlight ideas, symbols or social issues, or when the story is not literal.

practice.q: How could one production mix realism and non-realism?
practice.a: Realistic scenes with narration or projected titles between them.

practice.q: How does the laid-off worker scene change when performed in Brechtian style?
practice.a: The audience thinks about the economic system rather than feeling only for the worker.

practice.q: Why might absurdism appeal after World War II?
practice.a: It reflected a feeling that life had lost meaning.

misconceptions: Thinking realism is the only "good" acting
Thinking Brechtian theatre has no emotion
Thinking non-realism means random or careless
